newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader threatens to dissolve parliament.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader threatens to dissolve parliament.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, the fiery leader of Belarus, said on Tuesday he would dissolve parliament if the constitutional court refused to approve a referendum he wants to hold to boost his powers.
If the court, due to meet on Friday, ruled the poll illegal, "then I will dissolve the parliament," he told a meeting of war veterans broadcast in part on television late on Tuesday.
In typical style, the imposing, moustachioed former collective farm head swiped at his opponents in parliament, delighting the crowd of elderly war veterans who clapped warmly.
"With fresh forces they are continuing to work at destroying the referendum. A terrible battle is going on. They could not care less about the constitution, the law, the people," he said.
Lukashenko this month fell in line with deputies and the constitution, saying he would hold his vote on November 24 instead of November 7 as he had been insisting.
Deputies had already fixed the date of November 24 -- as is their right by the constitution -- for their own poll aimed at abolishing the post of president altogether.
Voters will now have to answer seven questions and decide between two draft constitutions proposed by Lukashenko and parliament which each rob the other of their authority.
Lukashenko says he won the right to dissolve parliament in a referendum in May 1995, when voters backed him overwhelmingly.
But his opponents, who accuse him of building a dictatorship, say that question was only consultative rather than legally binding and had no constitutional force.
Lukashenko has been battling a majority of deputies over the referendum and many other issues since he won a landslide victory on a platform of fighting crime in July 1994.
Since then he has suspended trade unions, closed newspapers and frozen the country's privatisation programme.
The 44-year-old president has drawn criticism from the West and lending bodies have halted credits to the former Soviet republic of about 10 million people pending faster reforms.
Lukashenko wants to use the referendum to extend his powers to allow him to appoint all criminal court judges, half the constitutional court and half the Central Electoral Commission.
If his new draft was approved he would recommence his five-year stay in power from the date of the vote, effectively extending his term without elections by more than two years.
